gloss_terse: Yimrah, a chief of the tribe of Asher mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles
gloss_readable: Yimrah appears only once in Scripture as a tribal leader within Asher's genealogical record. The name is preserved in the Greek tradition as Iamarē or Iemra, showing slight variation across manuscript families. As with many genealogical entries in Chronicles, this brief mention anchors a family line within Israel's tribal structure.

senses.1: A proper name designating an Asherite chief in 1 Chronicles 7:36. The single occurrence and genealogical context indicate a historical figure whose primary significance lies in maintaining tribal memory and lineage documentation within the Chronicler's comprehensive genealogical framework.

gloss_terse: Yanoach, a town in the extreme northern region of Israel conquered by Tiglath-Pileser III
gloss_readable: Yanoach was a northern Israelite settlement captured during the Assyrian campaigns of 2 Kings 15:29. Its exact location remains disputed among scholars, with proposals ranging from sites near Tyre to locations west of the upper Jordan. The town's inclusion in the list of conquered territories reflects the scope of Assyrian territorial expansion during this period.

senses.1: A place name referring to a northern Israelite town in 2 Kings 15:29, captured by Tiglath-Pileser III. The geographical uncertainty in modern scholarship (proposals include Hunin west of the upper Jordan) underscores how many biblical place names have lost their precise identification over millennia, though the conquest itself is historically attested.

gloss_terse: Young shoots or tender sprouts, used metaphorically in Ezekiel for Israel as a cedar
gloss_readable: This rare feminine plural form appears only in Ezekiel's allegory of the great cedar (17:4), where Israel is depicted as a tree whose tender shoots are plucked. The cross-linguistic evidence shows Romance languages favoring 'young shoot' or 'sprout' terminology, while the imagery evokes botanical vulnerability and potential growth. The metaphor captures both Israel's fragility and her promise.

senses.1: Denotes the tender young shoots or sprouts of a plant, specifically appearing in Ezekiel 17:4 within the extended metaphor of Israel as a cedar. The Spanish 'renuevos' and French 'jeune-pousse' both emphasize the botanical newness and tender quality, fitting the prophetic context of judgment upon Israel's leadership and future restoration.

gloss_terse: Foundation or beginning, though textual criticism suggests reading as a verb form in Ezra 7:9
gloss_readable: This hapax legomenon in Ezra 7:9 presents textual difficulties. BDB suggests that rather than the noun 'foundation of the ascent,' we should read the verb 'he founded' with Ezra as subject, following the Greek tradition. Such textual questions are common in post-exilic literature where Hebrew was undergoing transition. The underlying concept relates to establishing or beginning something.

senses.1: Appears to mean 'foundation' or 'beginning' in Ezra 7:9, though scholarly consensus favors emending to the verbal form 'he founded' based on Greek manuscript evidence. The uncertainty reflects the textual fluidity of Ezra-Nehemiah, where Persian-period Hebrew sometimes shows unusual forms that sparked interpretive traditions across language families.

gloss_terse: His foundation, referring to Zion in Psalm 87, with the city as the object of God's love
gloss_readable: This possessive form appears in Psalm 87:1, where God's foundation is established on the holy mountains. The parallelism with 'the gates of Zion' makes clear that the city itself is meant. The image evokes stability, divine choice, and permanence—Jerusalem as the place where God has set his immovable foundation. The multilingual glosses preserve the possessive and architectural metaphor.

senses.1: Means 'his foundation' in Psalm 87:1, referring to Zion as the city founded by God on the holy mountains. The architectural metaphor (German 'Grundfeste,' Spanish 'fundamento') emphasizes divine establishment and permanence, while the possessive suffix underscores God's personal choice and ownership of the holy city as his dwelling place.

gloss_terse: Uncertain form in Jeremiah 17:13, possibly related to departing or animal husbandry contexts
gloss_readable: This obscure term in Jeremiah 17:13 has uncertain meaning. The ketiv-qere variation and sparse glossing suggest textual difficulty. Spanish renders 'those who depart from me,' while other traditions leave it untranslated. The domain assignment to animal husbandry may reflect etymological speculation, but the context of Jeremiah 17 concerns those who turn away from the Lord as the fountain of living water.

senses.1: An uncertain Hebrew form in Jeremiah 17:13, where the Spanish tradition interprets it as 'those who depart from me' within the context of abandoning the Lord as the source of living water. The textual ambiguity and sparse cross-linguistic evidence indicate this is a crux interpretum where ancient translators struggled to establish clear meaning.

gloss_terse: One who reproves or finds fault, a faultfinder who contends (Job 40:2)
gloss_readable: This participial noun appears in God's challenge to Job: 'Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty?' The term captures the audacity of human criticism directed at divine wisdom and action. The Spanish 'disputará' (will he contend?) and English 'faultfinder' both preserve the confrontational tone, fitting the climactic divine speeches where God questions Job's qualification to critique the Creator's governance.

senses.1: Designates a person who reproves or criticizes, specifically in Job 40:2 where God challenges whether a mere faultfinder is qualified to contend with Shaddai. The term's rhetorical force lies in exposing the presumption of human judgment when directed against divine wisdom, a central theme in the divine speeches of Job 38-41.

gloss_terse: Passive form: it shall be poured or anointed, regarding sacred anointing oil (Exodus 30:32)
gloss_readable: This passive imperfect form appears in the regulations for holy anointing oil in Exodus 30:32. The text prohibits pouring this sacred oil on ordinary flesh, reserving it exclusively for tabernacle furnishings and consecrated persons. The verb's passive voice emphasizes the oil as subject—it shall not be poured in unauthorized contexts. Scholarly discussion includes whether this is passive Qal or Hophal.

senses.1: A passive verbal form meaning 'it shall be poured' in Exodus 30:32, within the prohibition against using sacred anointing oil for common purposes. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'será derramado,' French 'cela être versa') confirms the passive sense, emphasizing the oil's restricted sacred status in tabernacle worship.

gloss_terse: Iscah, daughter of Haran and sister of Milcah in Genesis 11
gloss_readable: Iscah appears in the genealogical record of Abraham's family as Haran's daughter and Milcah's sister. Her single mention in Genesis 11:29 situates her within the transitional generation between Terah's departure from Ur and Abraham's call. The Greek rendering Iescha preserves the name with slight phonetic adaptation. Her etymology remains uncertain.

senses.1: A feminine proper name in Genesis 11:29 designating the daughter of Haran and sister of Milcah in the patriarchal genealogy. The single biblical occurrence and uncertain etymology place Iscah among those family members mentioned to establish kinship networks in the pre-Abrahamic narrative.

gloss_terse: Ismachiah, a Levite overseer during Hezekiah's reforms, possibly meaning 'Yahweh sustains'
gloss_readable: Ismachiah served as a Levitical administrator under Hezekiah's reforms in 2 Chronicles 31:13. The name likely means 'Yahweh sustains,' though Gray suggests reading it as the simpler form found in related names. The Greek tradition renders it Samachia. His role in managing temple contributions reflects the organizational structure of Hezekiah's religious renewal.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 2 Chronicles 31:13 identifying a Levite involved in Hezekiah's temple administration. The theophoric element suggests divine sustenance or support, fitting the context of faithful stewardship during a period of covenant renewal and centralized worship reform in Judah.

gloss_terse: Was added (Hophal perfect), referring to Daniel's restored understanding in Daniel 4:36
gloss_readable: This Aramaic Hophal form describes the restoration of Daniel's reason after his period of divine judgment and humiliation. 'My understanding was added to me' marks the turning point when sanity returns. The passive voice emphasizes that restoration is received, not achieved—a gift following repentance. The form represents a characteristic Aramaism in biblical Aramaic portions.

senses.1: The Aramaic Hophal perfect 'was added' in Daniel 4:36, describing the restoration of Nebuchadnezzar's (or the speaker's) reason after the humbling period of madness. The passive construction highlights divine agency in restoration, with the Spanish 'me fue añadida' and French 'ajouter' preserving the sense of reception rather than self-achievement.

gloss_terse: Shall sweep away, carrying off the false refuge (Isaiah 28:17)
gloss_readable: In Isaiah's oracle against Judah's false security, this verb describes how hail will sweep away the refuge of lies. The imagery is meteorological and violent—divine judgment removing deceptive shelters. The Arabic cognate waʿā (to collect, gather) may suggest sweeping together and carrying off. Modern Arabic dialectal evidence from Palestinian usage supports this semantic field.

senses.1: Means 'shall sweep away' in Isaiah 28:17, where hail serves as God's instrument to remove the false refuge in which Jerusalem's leaders have trusted. The Spanish 'barrerá' (will sweep) and the Arabic cognate evidence both support the sense of forceful removal, fitting Isaiah's vivid judgment imagery against political alliances made in bad faith.

gloss_terse: Yeuel, a descendant of Zerah in the Chronicles genealogies
gloss_readable: Yeuel appears as a son of Zerah in 1 Chronicles 9:6, within the genealogical records of those who returned from exile. The name's etymology is uncertain, and Greek manuscript traditions show variation (Epeiēl, Ieeēl). Like many genealogical entries, this preserves tribal memory and lineage continuity across the traumatic disruption of the Babylonian exile.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 9:6 identifying a member of Zerah's line among the post-exilic returnees. The single occurrence and genealogical function mark Yeuel as part of the Chronicler's concern to document legitimate Israelite descent and tribal continuity despite exile.

gloss_terse: Yeuts, a Benjamite name in 1 Chronicles 8:10
gloss_readable: Yeuts appears in the Benjamite genealogies as one of the descendants listed in 1 Chronicles 8:10. The name's meaning is uncertain, and Greek traditions vary in their transliteration (Idōs, Ieous, Iōas). These genealogical records served to maintain tribal identity and legitimacy within the post-exilic community's self-understanding.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 8:10 within the Benjamite genealogical framework. The sparse attestation and uncertain etymology are typical of many names preserved solely for genealogical continuity, serving the Chronicler's broader purpose of establishing tribal legitimacy and historical rootedness.

gloss_terse: Barbarous or fierce, describing a foreign invading people in Isaiah 33:19
gloss_readable: This difficult Niphal participle describes the invading foreigners Isaiah promises will no longer be seen. The root meaning is uncertain—possibly 'making signs' or 'speaking unintelligibly,' hence 'barbarous,' or perhaps 'fierce' or 'arrogant.' The Spanish 'feroz' (fierce) captures one possibility. Context favors foreigners whose language is incomprehensible, fitting the parallel description of 'a people of obscure speech.'

senses.1: An adjective describing an invading foreign people in Isaiah 33:19, probably meaning 'barbarous' (speaking unintelligibly) or 'fierce.' The lexical uncertainty reflects the rare root, though context strongly suggests foreigners characterized by incomprehensible language and threatening demeanor, whom God will remove from Jerusalem's sight.

gloss_terse: Yaaziel, a Levite name in 1 Chronicles 15, possibly a textual variant of Aziel or Uzziel
gloss_readable: Yaaziel appears among the Levites appointed for musical service in 1 Chronicles 15:18. Verse 20 lists the same individual as Aziel, and scholars suggest both may be textual corruptions of Uzziel. Such variations are common in Chronicles' genealogical and organizational lists, where copyist errors or genuine name variants create minor discrepancies across parallel passages.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 15:18 designating a Levite musician, though probably a textual variant or error for Aziel (v. 20) or Uzziel, as suggested by Gray. The Greek rendering Oziēl supports this view, illustrating how manuscript transmission could generate variant forms of the same name.

gloss_terse: He wrapped or covered me, used in Isaiah 61:10 of being clothed with salvation's robe
gloss_readable: This verb appears in Isaiah's triumphant declaration: 'He has covered me with the robe of righteousness.' The imagery is sartorial and ceremonial, evoking priestly or royal investiture. The parallel verb 'clothed me with garments of salvation' reinforces the metaphor. Some scholars suggest reading this as a form of the more common ʿāṭâ, though the Qal perfect form here is distinctive.

senses.1: Means 'he wrapped me' or 'he covered me' in Isaiah 61:10, describing God's action of clothing the speaker with righteousness like a ceremonial robe. The Spanish 'me cubrió' preserves the covering imagery, fitting the broader context of divine vindication and restoration where garments symbolize transformed status before God and the nations.

gloss_terse: Have consulted or taken counsel (Aramaic Ithpael), reflexive counsel-taking in Daniel 6
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb describes the officials who conspired together to trap Daniel in Daniel 6:7. The Ithpael stem conveys reciprocal action—they counseled with one another. The context is political conspiracy, where collective deliberation produces the decree designed to ensnare Daniel in his faithfulness to God. The multilingual evidence confirms the consultative sense.

senses.1: An Aramaic Ithpael perfect meaning 'have consulted' or 'took counsel together' in Daniel 6:7, describing the collaborative conspiracy of officials against Daniel. The reciprocal force of the Ithpael stem (they counseled with each other) fits the narrative of collective scheming to manipulate the king's decree against Daniel's prayer life.

gloss_terse: Ya'khan, a Gadite name in 1 Chronicles 5:13
gloss_readable: Ya'khan appears in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 5:13. The name's single occurrence and uncertain etymology are typical of tribal genealogical records. Greek manuscript traditions show variation (Chima, Iacha), reflecting the challenges of transliterating Hebrew names into Greek. The genealogy serves to establish Gadite territorial and familial claims.

senses.1: A masculine proper name identifying a Gadite in 1 Chronicles 5:13. The brief mention within the genealogical framework of the Transjordanian tribes preserves family memory and territorial legitimacy, though Ya'khan himself receives no narrative elaboration beyond his place in the lineage structure.

gloss_terse: A graceful doe, used figuratively for a wife in Proverbs 5:19
gloss_readable: This feminine noun appears in the hendiadys 'a loving doe and a graceful gazelle,' describing the wife in Proverbs 5:19. The imagery evokes beauty, grace, and desirability, with the gazelle/doe pair common in wisdom and poetic literature for depicting feminine charm. The Spanish 'gacela' and the parallel with 'loving hind' both preserve the gentle, swift, graceful connotations of the animal imagery.

senses.1: Denotes a graceful doe or female mountain goat in Proverbs 5:19, used metaphorically for a wife. The pairing with 'loving hind' creates poetic parallelism emphasizing beauty and desirability, typical of Proverbs' positive commendation of faithful marital love as opposed to the adultery warned against in the surrounding context.

gloss_terse: Ya'nai, a Gadite name in 1 Chronicles 5:12
gloss_readable: Ya'nai appears among the Gadite leaders in 1 Chronicles 5:12, within the genealogical and territorial records of the Transjordanian tribes. The name's etymology is uncertain, and the single occurrence provides no narrative context beyond genealogical placement. Such names anchor family lines within tribal memory and territorial claims.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 5:12 identifying a Gadite chief. The genealogical function preserves tribal identity and leadership succession, though Ya'nai receives no further narrative development. The name participates in the Chronicler's comprehensive documentation of Israel's tribal structure.

gloss_terse: In weariness or swift flight, describing Gabriel's manner in Daniel 9:21
gloss_readable: This difficult term in Daniel 9:21 has sparked interpretive debate. The traditional view sees weariness from winged flight (Gabriel arriving weary), while others render it simply 'in swift flight.' The Spanish 'en vuelo' (in flight) and French 'forme' show divergent interpretations. Lagarde identified it as an Aramaism. The context describes Gabriel's rapid arrival during Daniel's prayer.

senses.1: An uncertain term in Daniel 9:21, probably meaning 'in weariness' or possibly 'in swift flight,' describing Gabriel's arrival to Daniel. The phrase 'caused to fly swiftly in weariness' suggests the angel's rapid transit from heaven, though the exact nuance remains debated. Cross-linguistic variation reflects the exegetical uncertainty surrounding this hapax expression.

gloss_terse: Ya'aqovah, a Simeonite name in 1 Chronicles 4:36
gloss_readable: Ya'aqovah appears in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:36. The name may be a variant or derivative form related to Jacob (Ya'aqov), though the precise etymology is uncertain. Greek traditions vary (Iōkaba, Iakaba, Iekeba), showing the transliteration challenges. The genealogical context establishes Simeonite family lineage and territorial associations.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 4:36 within Simeonite genealogical records. The possible connection to the root meaning 'heel' or 'supplant' (as in Jacob) remains speculative, and the name's primary function is genealogical—preserving a family line within Simeon's tribal structure.

gloss_terse: Ya'aqan, an Edomite name in 1 Chronicles 1:42, parallel to Akan in Genesis 36:27
gloss_readable: Ya'aqan appears in the Edomite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1:42, parallel to Akan in Genesis 36:27. The name also appears in the wilderness itinerary as 'wells of Bene-yaaqan.' Greek manuscript traditions show variation (Ōnan, Iaakan), typical of proper name transmission. The dual occurrence (personal and place name) reflects common ancient Near Eastern naming practices.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 1:42 identifying an Edomite descendant of Seir, parallel to Akan in Genesis 36:27. The name's appearance in both personal and geographical contexts (wells of Bene-yaaqan) illustrates how ancestral names often became attached to tribal territories and landmarks in ancient Near Eastern genealogical memory.

gloss_terse: In the honeycomb of, a construct form appearing in 1 Samuel 14:27
gloss_readable: This rare construct form appears when Jonathan dips his staff into the honeycomb in 1 Samuel 14:27. The phrase 'honeycomb of honey' uses construct syntax to specify the forest honey available during the battle with the Philistines. The multilingual glosses consistently preserve the honeycomb imagery, though some Germanic traditions leave it transliterated, suggesting lexical uncertainty.

senses.1: A construct form meaning 'honeycomb of' in 1 Samuel 14:27, appearing in the narrative of Jonathan's unwitting violation of Saul's oath. The phrase 'in the honeycomb of honey' emphasizes the forest honey's natural abundance, contrasting with the enforced fast that weakened Israel's troops during battle.

gloss_terse: Mount Yearim, a geographical location in Joshua 15:10 identified with Kesalon
gloss_readable: Mount Yearim appears in the border description of Judah in Joshua 15:10, where it is explained as equivalent to Kesalon (modern Kesla), northeast of Beth-shemesh. The name means 'mount of forests,' and Greek traditions render it as 'city of Iarain.' The geographical marker helps define tribal boundaries in the allotment narratives.

senses.1: A place name in Joshua 15:10 designating a mountain on Judah's northern border, identified with Kesalon (modern Kesla). The reference to 'mount of forests' connects to the root for forest/woodland, and the boundary description helps establish the territorial limits of Judah's inheritance in the conquest allocation.

gloss_terse: Yaareshyah, a Benjamite name in 1 Chronicles 8:27
gloss_readable: Yaareshyah appears in the Benjamite genealogical records of 1 Chronicles 8:27. The name's etymology is uncertain, and Greek manuscript traditions show variation (Iasaraia, Iarasia, Iersia). These genealogical lists in Chronicles function to maintain tribal identity and legitimacy, particularly important for the Benjamite community's post-exilic self-understanding.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 8:27 within Benjamin's genealogical framework. The single occurrence and uncertain etymology are typical of genealogical preservation, where names maintain family memory and tribal continuity even when their original meanings have become obscure.

gloss_terse: Yifdeiyah, a Benjamite name in 1 Chronicles 8:25, possibly related to redemption
gloss_readable: Yifdeiyah appears in Benjamin's genealogy in 1 Chronicles 8:25. BDB cross-references the root pādâ (to redeem), suggesting the name may mean 'Yahweh redeems.' Such theophoric names were common in Israelite naming practices, expressing theological convictions about God's character and activity. The genealogical context serves to establish legitimate Benjamite lineage.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 8:25 identifying a Benjamite. The likely etymology from the root 'redeem' suggests a theophoric name meaning 'Yahweh redeems,' reflecting the common practice of encoding theological affirmations within personal names that commemorated divine attributes or family circumstances.

gloss_terse: Gasping for breath (Hithpael), describing a woman in labor in Jeremiah 4:31
gloss_readable: This Hithpael form describes Daughter Zion gasping for breath like a woman in her first labor in Jeremiah 4:31. The reflexive stem emphasizes the involuntary, desperate nature of the breathing. The image is one of extreme distress and vulnerability, fitting Jeremiah's vivid description of coming judgment. The verb is a by-form of the more common pûaḥ (to puff, breathe).

senses.1: A Hithpael imperfect meaning 'gasping for breath' in Jeremiah 4:31, used of Daughter Zion's desperate condition under judgment. The reflexive stem and the comparison to a woman in first labor both heighten the imagery of involuntary distress, while the Spanish 'jadea' (gasps, pants) preserves the labored breathing connotation.

gloss_terse: One breathing out violence, a participial phrase in Psalm 27:12
gloss_readable: This rare participial adjective describes enemies who 'breathe out' or 'puff out' violence in Psalm 27:12. The imagery suggests menacing intent expressed through speech or aggressive posture. The construct relationship 'one breathing out violence' captures the threatening demeanor of David's adversaries. Spanish 'el que respira' (one who breathes) and French 'soufflant' (blowing) both preserve the breathing metaphor.

senses.1: A participial adjective meaning 'one breathing out' or 'puffing out' in Psalm 27:12, used with 'violence' to describe threatening enemies. The image evokes aggressive speech or menacing posture, fitting the lament context where David seeks protection from adversaries whose very bearing communicates hostile intent.

gloss_terse: The Japhletites, a clan or family on the southwestern border of Ephraim
gloss_readable: The Japhletites appear as a gentilics (clan designation) marking Ephraim's southwestern border in Joshua 16:3. The definite article with the gentilic functions as a collective noun—'the territory of the Japhletites.' Greek traditions vary (Aphtaleim, Iephalti), and the group's identity beyond this border reference is uncertain. Such markers were crucial for tribal land allocation.

senses.1: A gentilic (clan designation) in Joshua 16:3 marking the southwestern border of Ephraim's tribal allotment. The use of the definite article creates a collective sense—'the Japhletite territory'—functioning as a geographical landmark in the distribution of the promised land among the tribes.

gloss_terse: Was completed or finished (Aramaic Shafel), describing the temple's completion in Ezra 6:15
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb describes the completion of the Second Temple in Ezra 6:15. Scholars identify it as a Shafel (causative) stem of a root borrowed from Assyrian (šûṣû, bring out to completion). Textual critics suggest reading the plural 'they finished' rather than singular, following some Greek manuscripts. The completion marks the culmination of the post-exilic community's restoration efforts.

senses.1: An Aramaic verbal form meaning 'was completed' in Ezra 6:15, describing the Second Temple's construction finish. The form represents an Assyrian loanword in Aramaic (from yṣʾ/wṣʾ), and textual evidence suggests reading a plural 'they finished' with the community as subject, emphasizing the collective achievement of the restoration generation.

gloss_terse: To make certain or gain certainty (Aramaic Pael infinitive), in Daniel 7:19
gloss_readable: This Aramaic Pael infinitive appears in Daniel's request for certainty concerning the fourth beast in Daniel 7:19. The causative stem emphasizes making certain or establishing truth about something. The context is apocalyptic vision and interpretation—Daniel seeks definitive understanding of symbolic imagery. The Spanish 'saber la verdad' (to know the truth) captures the epistemological thrust.

senses.1: An Aramaic Pael infinitive meaning 'to make certain' or 'to gain certainty' in Daniel 7:19, used with the preposition 'concerning' to express Daniel's desire for definitive understanding of the fourth beast. The causative stem underscores the active pursuit of clarity regarding apocalyptic symbolism whose meaning requires divine disclosure.

gloss_terse: Tsokhar (ketiv Yitschar), a name in Judah's genealogy in 1 Chronicles 4:7
gloss_readable: This name appears in Judah's genealogy in 1 Chronicles 4:7 with a ketiv-qere variation: the text reads Yitschar while the margin suggests Tsokhar. The latter form matches the name of Ephron's father (Genesis 23:8) and a Simeonite ancestor. Greek traditions render it Saaar. Such textual variants in Chronicles' genealogies likely reflect manuscript transmission differences.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 4:7, where the ketiv reads Yitschar but qere suggests Tsokhar (matching names in Genesis 23:8 and Exodus 6:15). The textual variation illustrates scribal uncertainty, possibly reflecting genuine name variations across family branches or copyist error in genealogical transmission.

gloss_terse: My forms or limbs, referring to body parts in Job 17:7
gloss_readable: This rare plural form with possessive suffix means 'my forms' or 'my members' in Job 17:7, where Job describes his deteriorating physical condition. The context speaks of eyes growing dim and bodily members wasting away like shadows. The imagery is somatic and visceral, typical of Job's complaints about his physical suffering. The root relates to forming or fashioning.

senses.1: A masculine plural noun with first-person suffix meaning 'my forms' or 'my limbs' in Job 17:7, referring to Job's body parts or members that have wasted away like shadows. The Spanish 'mis miembros' (my members) preserves the somatic reference, fitting Job's lament over comprehensive physical deterioration under suffering.

gloss_terse: Yitsri, chief of a Levitical choir in 1 Chronicles 25:11
gloss_readable: Yitsri appears as the leader of one of the Levitical singing divisions in 1 Chronicles 25:11. The name may relate to the root yāṣar (to form, fashion). The context is David's organization of temple musicians into twenty-four courses, each assigned by lot. Yitsri's division represents one component of the elaborate worship structure the Chronicler attributes to David's preparations.

senses.1: A masculine proper name in 1 Chronicles 25:11 designating a chief musician among the Levitical temple choirs. The organizational context reflects the Chronicler's emphasis on ordered worship, with Yitsri's division forming one of the twenty-four courses that rotated musical service in the sanctuary.

gloss_terse: The Jezerites, a Naphtalite clan descended from Jezer (Numbers 26:49)
gloss_readable: The Jezerites appear as a gentilic designation in the census of Numbers 26:49, representing the clan descended from Jezer son of Naphtali. The definite article creates a collective sense—'the Jezerite clan.' Such census lists were crucial for tribal organization, military muster, and land distribution. The gentilic functions to organize families within the larger tribal structure.

senses.1: A gentilic (clan designation) in Numbers 26:49 referring to the descendants of Jezer within the tribe of Naphtali. The census context uses this patronymic form to organize and enumerate family groups for military and territorial purposes in Israel's tribal structure during the wilderness period.

gloss_terse: In Yeqavtseel (Kabzeel), a town in southern Judah, appearing in Nehemiah 11:25
gloss_readable: Yeqavtseel appears with the preposition and locative he in Nehemiah 11:25 as one of the towns where returned exiles settled. The name means 'God gathers' and is parallel to Kabzeel in earlier texts (Joshua 15:21, 2 Samuel 23:20). The resettlement lists in Nehemiah document the repopulation of Judean territory after the Babylonian exile.

senses.1: A place name with locative prefix in Nehemiah 11:25, referring to Kabzeel in southern Judah where post-exilic Jews resettled. The name 'God gathers' takes on poignant significance in the exile-return context, as the gathered community reoccupies ancestral towns that had lain desolate during the captivity.

gloss_terse: To the burning of fire, a construct phrase in Daniel 7:11
gloss_readable: This Aramaic construct phrase appears in Daniel's vision of the fourth beast being given 'to the burning of fire' in Daniel 7:11. The imagery is apocalyptic and judicial—divine judgment executed through fire. The construct relationship links 'burning' with 'fire' for emphasis. The context depicts the beast's destruction following the Ancient of Days' judgment scene.

senses.1: An Aramaic construct phrase meaning 'to the burning of fire' in Daniel 7:11, describing the fourth beast's destruction in apocalyptic vision. The emphatic construction intensifies the imagery of divine judgment, with the Spanish 'a ardor de' (to the burning of) and French 'incendie' (conflagration) both preserving the judicial fire motif.

gloss_terse: Yokdeam, a city in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:56), site unknown
gloss_readable: Yokdeam appears in the territorial allotment of Judah as a town in the hill country in Joshua 15:56. Its precise location remains unidentified in modern scholarship. Greek manuscript traditions show variation (Iareikam, Iekdaam, Ieknaam), typical of place name transmission. The town is part of Judah's inheritance but receives no further biblical elaboration.

senses.1: A place name in Joshua 15:56 designating a town in Judah's hill country allotment, whose precise location has been lost to history. The single occurrence and lack of modern identification illustrate how many biblical place names remain unrecovered despite the preservation of territorial boundary descriptions in Joshua.
